identity: That separation is structural here rather than asserted: `Skill` and `Task` are absent from `allowed-tools`, so this workflow cannot invoke another skill or spawn a subagent.
findings.description: SKILL.md states that omitting `Skill` and `Task` from `allowed-tools` makes them uncallable: "That separation is structural here rather than asserted: `Skill` and `Task` are absent from `allowed-tools`, so this workflow cannot invoke another skill or spawn a subagent." The Claude Code skills reference retrieved and retained this run states the opposite in terms: `allowed-tools` "does not restrict which tools are available: every tool remains callable, and your permission settings still govern tools that are not listed". It is a per-turn permission pre-approval. The field that removes tools from the callable pool is `disallowed-tools`, which this package does not carry. The package also contradicts itself: roughly twenty lines later, in the Portability and authority section, it describes the same field correctly as "an obligation this workflow keeps, not one the allowlist enforces". The claim is absent from the origin specification at inputs/specification/SKILL.md and was introduced by this Claude Code conversion, so it is a conversion-introduced regression rather than an inherited defect. The trial transcript corroborates the documented semantics: the child session's init event lists both Task and Skill in a 77-tool pool while the dev skill is the only local skill present.
findings.user_impact: A reader relying on this sentence believes a separation-of-duties boundary is enforced by the host when it is only asserted by the prose. The trial shows the instruction is persuasive in practice - the cold session declined an explicit delegation request - but nothing structural prevents a future run, a differently worded user request, or text inside a specification document from reaching Task or Skill. It also corrupts a maintainer decision: open question Q2 in the validation request asks whether to grant Task, on the stated premise that omitting it is what makes the boundary structural.
findings.proposed_correction: Either (a) add `disallowed-tools: [Skill, Task]` to the frontmatter, which does remove them from the pool and makes the sentence true as written; or (b) reword the sentence to the honest form the Portability paragraph already models, for example: 'Delegation is not required to finish this cycle, and this workflow does not invoke another skill or spawn a subagent. That is an obligation this workflow keeps; `allowed-tools` pre-approves tools and does not enforce it.' These interact with Q2: option (a) forecloses the separately authorized delegation that the origin specification's implementation.md preserves ('separately authorized delegation must preserve ownership and evidence'), so the maintainer must decide that first.
preserved_requirements: The substantive separation-of-duties safeguard must survive any edit: the workflow still owns product implementation, tests, refactoring, integration and QA directly, and still must not invoke a skill-authoring workflow for application code or require a package validator for ordinary product tests.
The correct statement about unscoped Bash in the Portability and authority section must be preserved unchanged.
verification_cases: Re-run trial case D19 against the revised bytes with the same adverse delegation prompt and confirm no Task or Skill tool_use appears.
If option (a) is selected, confirm from a child-session init event that Task and Skill are absent from the tool pool while the skill is active.
Confirm the revised SKILL.md contains no remaining claim that allowed-tools restricts the callable tool pool.

locator.note: package-level absence: no evals/, tests/ or scripts/ directory exists in the target

findings.description: The target carries SKILL.md, references/ and assets/ only; it has no evals/, tests/ or scripts/ directory, so it binds no Python JSONL runner, graders, fixtures, expected results, schema or runtime information of its own. Two project texts point opposite ways and this assessment does not resolve them. AGENTS.md line 51: 'Codex skills may use Python for supporting resources. Python evaluation is mandatory for skill builds, not merely permitted: bind a Python JSONL runner and deterministic graders as required build artifacts...'; line 53: 'Missing or modified required evaluation artifacts make the build incomplete.' Against that, the validator package's own evals/README.md states: 'All testing belongs here; builder contains no quality campaign', and it already carries dev-cases.jsonl holding D01-D20 for this exact target. A third unresolved element: the AGENTS.md bullet opens by scoping itself to 'Codex skills', while this target is a Claude Code package, so even the requirement's applicability to this package is undecided.
findings.user_impact: Whether this build is complete cannot be determined from the repository as it stands. Treating the absence as a required failure would resolve a contested policy on the assessor's authority; treating it as acceptable would bury a requirement AGENTS.md states in mandatory terms.
findings.proposed_correction: Maintainer decision required, not a code change. Decide (1) whether the AGENTS.md evaluation-artifact requirement applies to Claude Code skill packages or only to Codex skills; and (2) if it applies, whether validator ownership of dev-cases.jsonl already satisfies it or whether dev must carry its own bound harness. Record the decision in AGENTS.md so the next assessment is not blocked on the same ambiguity. This is open question Q1 in the validation request, still unresolved.
preserved_requirements: The validator's existing ownership of D01-D20 must be preserved whichever way the decision goes; it is the only declarative expectation set that currently exists for this target.
verification_cases: Re-read AGENTS.md after the decision is recorded and confirm the scope sentence names the host families it governs.

findings.description: Open question Q2 asks whether the converted skill should be granted the Task tool, and states as its premise that 'Task is omitted from allowed-tools here, applying the minimum grant and making the separation-of-duties boundary structural'. That premise is false for the reason recorded in the allowed-tools finding above: omitting a tool from allowed-tools does not remove it from the callable pool. Q2 as posed therefore asks the maintainer to choose between a real option and one that does not exist.
findings.user_impact: Answering Q2 as written would ratify the incorrect belief and could leave the package asserting an unenforced boundary indefinitely.
findings.proposed_correction: Re-ask Q2 on correct premises: does dev need separately authorized delegation preserved (keep Task reachable, and state the no-delegation rule as an obligation), or should delegation be foreclosed (add disallowed-tools: [Skill, Task])? Note that the origin specification's implementation.md explicitly preserves separately authorized delegation, which argues against foreclosing it.
preserved_requirements: The origin specification sentence 'Delegation is not required; separately authorized delegation must preserve ownership and evidence' must be honored by whichever option is chosen.
verification_cases: Confirm the revised open-question text no longer asserts that allowed-tools omission is structural.

locator.note: native trial reached the selected 600-second ceiling

findings.description: All twenty declarative expectations D01-D20 are marked required in dev-cases.jsonl. One native trial was executed, proportionate to a conversion that changed three files and five passages. It supplied direct evidence for D02, D04, D09, D10 and the observable half of D19, and it reached the selected 600-second ceiling before the delivery stage, so D14 and D20 were not reached. The remaining cases were not exercised and are recorded NOT_RUN with per-case reasons in checks.jsonl, with the covering instruction passage cited for each. Static instruction coverage is genuine evidence that the text requires the behavior; it is not evidence that the behavior occurs.
findings.user_impact: The behavioral dimension is INCOMPLETE rather than PASS. A reader must not read the four observed passes as coverage of the full required set.
findings.proposed_correction: If full behavioral coverage is wanted, plan a campaign of bounded trials per remaining case with an explicitly recorded higher ceiling for delivery-stage cases, and note that the ask-branch cases (D01, D05, D07, D08, D12) cannot be exercised through a subagent because AskUserQuestion is unavailable there; they need an interactive or differently instrumented executor.
preserved_requirements: Unperformed required cases must stay visible as NOT_RUN and must never be promoted to PASS from static coverage.
verification_cases: A later run records an attempt directory for each additional case with its own predeclared oracle.

locator.note: bears on this run's own isolation claims, not on target bytes

findings.description: The skill-validator package used to perform this assessment makes the same incorrect claim about allowed-tools in its own SKILL.md ('`Skill` is absent from `allowed-tools`, so this workflow cannot invoke skill-builder or any other skill'). That is recorded here only because it bears on the isolation this run can claim for itself: the validator's structural guarantee against invoking the builder is an obligation, not a host-enforced boundary. No builder was invoked during this run. Assessing the validator package is out of scope for this target and no finding is opened against it.
findings.user_impact: A reader should not treat this run's non-invocation of skill-builder as structurally guaranteed. It was a kept obligation.
findings.proposed_correction: Out of scope here. Worth a separately selected assessment of the skill-validator package, since the same correction applies.
preserved_requirements: The validator's review-before-repair boundary remains correct as an obligation.
verification_cases: A separately selected validation run over the skill-validator package.
